bibl.title: Last of the naval triumphs: revisiting some key Actian honours.
bibl.seg: Frederik Juliaan Vervaet & Christopher J. Dart, Last of the naval triumphs: revisiting some key Actian honours.
bibl.note: In 29 B.C., after his victories over Marcus Antonius and Cleopatra at Actium and in Egypt, Caesar Octavi(an)us returned to Rome as the uncontested master of the Roman world. He did so in a carefully managed pageant that culminated with his triple triumph on 13, 14 and 15 Sextilis (the month later renamed Augustus in his honour). The first day was the triumph over the Pannonians and the Dalmatians, the Iapydes and their neighbours, and some German and Gallic tribes; the second day commemorated the naval victory at Actium; the third and final triumph, the most costly and magnificent of them all, was over Egypt. Dio clarifies that the Egyptian spoils proved so rich and bountiful that they covered the expense and lustre of all three triumphal processions.
